procedural_history.impugned_order: Award dated May 24, 1963, in Industrial Dispute No. 5 of 1962, published in the Orissa Gazette dated June 14, 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not applicable. The case originated in the Labour Court, not the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Management of Utkal Machinery Ltd. appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the Labour Court's award. The Supreme Court modified the Labour Court's award to some extent and allowed the appeal to that extent.

directions: The award of the Labour Court dated May 24, 1963 is modified.
The respondent should be granted a sum of Rs. 4,800 as compensation.
The respondent should also be paid 6% interest from the date of order of the Labour Court till the date of payment.
There will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal has the power to inquire into an employee's termination to determine if it is mala fide, an act of victimisation, or an unfair labour practice, even when the management claims it is a simple discharge under the contract.

facts: An employee's services were terminated by the management.
The management claimed the termination was a simple discharge under the contract, justified by the employee's unsatisfactory work during her probation period.
The employee alleged that the termination was improper, mala fide (in bad faith), and an act of victimisation.
The dispute was referred to an Industrial Tribunal for adjudication.
law: The Supreme Court established that while a management has the contractual right to terminate an employee's services, this power must be exercised in good faith (bona fide).
An Industrial Tribunal is not bound by the form of the termination order and has the power to inquire into the substance of the matter.

The Tribunal can investigate whether the termination was a bona fide exercise of contractual power or if it was actually mala fide, an act of victimisation, an unfair labour practice, or so capricious and unreasonable that it suggests ulterior motives.
application: The Court applied this principle by examining the Tribunal's actions. The Tribunal had investigated the management's claim that the employee's work was unsatisfactory.
The Tribunal found that the management provided no evidence—either through witnesses or documents—to prove the employee's work was unsatisfactory.
In the absence of any evidence to support the management's stated reason, the Tribunal concluded that the discharge was not a genuine exercise of contractual power but was punitive and mala fide.
The Supreme Court agreed with the Tribunal's finding, holding that the discharge was indeed mala fide under the circumstances.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an Industrial Tribunal has the power to look behind a termination order, even one that appears to be a simple discharge under a contract. The Tribunal can inquire into the true nature of the termination to determine if it was a bona fide exercise of power or if it was actually mala fide, an act of victimisation, or an unfair labour practice. If the Tribunal finds the termination was not made in good faith, it can interfere and grant relief to the employee.

issue.issue_text: Whether the discharge of an employee for 'unsatisfactory work' without holding a proper inquiry constitutes a punitive dismissal for misconduct, thereby justifying the Tribunal's interference.

facts: An employee was discharged by her employer, who claimed her work was 'unsatisfactory' and that the termination was in accordance with her employment contract.
The employee alleged that the termination was improper, mala fide, and an act of victimisation.
The employer did not have any Standing Orders that defined or provided a procedure for dealing with misconduct.
law: An Industrial Tribunal can interfere with a management's termination order if it is found to be mala fide, an act of victimisation, an unfair labour practice, or so capricious as to suggest an ulterior motive.
In the absence of a company's Standing Order defining misconduct, terminating an employee for 'unsatisfactory work' can be treated as a punishment for misconduct.
If a discharge is tantamount to a punishment for misconduct, the employer is required to hold a proper inquiry before terminating the employee.
application: The Court determined that since the company had no Standing Orders, the reason given for the discharge—'unsatisfactory work'—should be treated as an allegation of misconduct.
Consequently, the discharge was not a simple termination of contract but was punitive in nature, as it was a punishment for this alleged misconduct.
Because the discharge was punitive, the management was obligated to conduct a proper inquiry before dismissing the employee, which it failed to do.

The Court also noted that the management failed to produce any evidence, either during the termination process or before the Labour Court, to substantiate its claim that the employee's work was actually unsatisfactory.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that discharging the employee for 'unsatisfactory work' without a proper inquiry was a punitive dismissal for misconduct. This failure to hold an inquiry, combined with a complete lack of evidence to support the employer's claim, rendered the termination mala fide. Therefore, the Tribunal was justified in interfering with the management's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the award of two years' salary as compensation to the discharged employee was justified in the circumstances of the case.

facts: The employee (respondent) had worked for the company for a short period of less than 5 months.
The Industrial Tribunal had awarded her two years' salary (Rs. 9,600) as compensation.
The employee did not have to give up a previous job to take this position.

The Tribunal had relied on a precedent (Assam Oil Co. Ltd. v. Its workmen), but in that case, the employee had worked for two years and the compensation amount was based on a concession by the company's lawyer, not a judicial determination.
law: The amount of compensation awarded to a wrongfully discharged employee must be justified by the specific circumstances of the case.
application: The Supreme Court found that an award of two years' salary was "exorbitant" for an employee who had only served for about 5 months.
The Court distinguished the facts of this case from the precedent relied upon by the lower tribunal, highlighting the much shorter service period in the present case.
The Court explicitly stated that there were "no special circumstances" in this case that would justify such a high compensation award.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the award of two years' salary was not justified. It found the amount to be exorbitant given the employee's short period of service and the lack of any special circumstances. Therefore, the Court reduced the compensation to Rs. 4,800, which is equivalent to one year's salary.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Industrial Tribunal has the power to inquire into an employee's termination to determine if it is mala fide, an act of victimisation, or an unfair labour practice, even when the management claims it is a simple discharge under the contract.
appellant_arguments: The termination was not a dismissal for misconduct but a simple discharge in terms of the contract.
The management's order should not be treated as a punitive dismissal for misconduct, and therefore, the Tribunal should not interfere.
respondent_arguments: The discharge from service was mala fide, as there was a complete absence of evidence regarding the alleged unsatisfactory work.
The termination was punitive in character, justifying the Tribunal's inquiry into the matter.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the discharge of an employee for 'unsatisfactory work' without holding a proper inquiry constitutes a punitive dismissal for misconduct, thereby justifying the Tribunal's interference.
appellant_arguments: The employee was not dismissed for misconduct but was simply discharged under the terms of her contract.
The employee was on probation for 6 months, during which her services could be terminated without notice or reason.
respondent_arguments: The discharge for 'unsatisfactory work' was tantamount to a punishment for alleged misconduct.
As the discharge was a punishment for misconduct, the management was not justified in terminating the service without holding a proper inquiry.
The employee denied ever receiving a letter stating she was on probation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the award of two years' salary as compensation to the discharged employee was justified in the circumstances of the case.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the compensation awarded by the Labour Court was excessive by appealing against the award.
respondent_arguments: The respondent did not appear, but her position would have been to uphold the original award of the Labour Court.

cases.case_name: Assam Oil Co. Ltd. v. Its workmen
cases.principle: An Industrial Tribunal is competent to inquire whether an order of termination was made in the bona fide exercise of a power conferred by contract. The Tribunal can interfere if the order is found to be mala fide, amounts to victimization or an unfair labor practice, or is so capricious or unreasonable as to suggest it was passed for ulterior motives.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When the validity of an employee's termination is challenged in an industrial adjudication, it is competent for the Industrial Tribunal to inquire whether the order of termination was a bona fide exercise of the power conferred by the contract. The Tribunal will not interfere if the power was exercised in good faith, but it can interfere and provide relief if the termination is mala fide, amounts to victimization, is an unfair labor practice, or is so capricious or unreasonable as to infer it was passed for ulterior motives.
obiter: In the absence of any Standing Order, the unsatisfactory work of an employee may be treated as misconduct, and a discharge for such work can be considered a punishment for alleged misconduct.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the management's termination of the employee, though framed as a simple discharge for 'unsatisfactory work' under the contract, was in substance a punitive dismissal for alleged misconduct. Because the management failed to hold a proper inquiry and, more importantly, failed to produce any evidence whatsoever to substantiate the claim of unsatisfactory work, the termination was deemed to be mala fide, justifying the Industrial Tribunal's interference. However, the compensation awarded was found to be excessive and was reduced.
legal_tests_applied: An Industrial Tribunal is competent to inquire whether an order of termination has been effected in the bona fide exercise of the power conferred by the contract. The Tribunal can interfere if the order is mala fide, amounts to victimisation or an unfair labour practice, or is so capricious or unreasonable as to lead to the inference that it was passed for ulterior motives.
why_appellant_lost: The Court determined that discharging an employee for 'unsatisfactory work' is tantamount to punishment for misconduct, especially in the absence of any Standing Orders defining misconduct. The Court stated: "In the absence of any Standing Order the unsatisfactory work of an employee may be treated as misconduct and when the respondent was discharged according to the management for unsatisfactory work it should be taken that her discharge was tantamount to punishment for an alleged misconduct."

Because the discharge was deemed a punishment for misconduct, the management was obligated to hold a proper inquiry before terminating the employee, which it failed to do. "If this conclusion is correct the management was not justified in discharging the respondent from service without holding a proper enquiry."

The appellant failed to produce any evidence, either during the termination process or before the Labour Court, to prove that the respondent's work was actually unsatisfactory. "Even before the Labour Court there was no evidence adduced on behalf of the management to show that the work of the respondent was unsatisfactory. Two witnesses were examined on behalf of the management but neither uttered a word about it."

The complete lack of evidence led the Court to conclude that the management's action was not in good faith. "in the face of complete absence of evidence in regard to unsatisfactory work of the respondent the discharge of the respondent from service was ma/a fide."
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the termination was not a simple contractual discharge but a punitive action requiring due process. The Court agreed that the reason given, 'unsatisfactory work', constituted an allegation of misconduct.
The respondent's position was vindicated by the management's total failure to substantiate its claim of her poor performance, which proved the termination was mala fide.
The Court affirmed the Tribunal's jurisdiction to look beyond the form of the termination order to its true substance, thereby protecting the employee from a disguised punitive dismissal.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the policy that an employer's contractual power to terminate an employee is not absolute and is subject to judicial review by an Industrial Tribunal to prevent abuse. The Tribunal has the power and duty to determine if the termination is a bona fide exercise of power or if it is a colorable exercise of power intended to victimize an employee or constitute an unfair labour practice.
